screens.title: Advanced Monitoring and Troubleshooting Scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move beyond simple dashboards and learn how to investigate complex performance problems across Azure databases. You will learn to use Kusto Query Language to correlate metrics and logs, to identify which queries or resources caused spikes, and to extract deadlock graphs from diagnostic streams. We’ll look at how resource contention can hide behind fast single-query timings, why distributed tracing is essential in microservices, and how custom metrics and logs let you observe behaviors not exposed by default telemetry. A practical outcome is capacity planning: using trend analysis to decide when to scale up or scale out before production impact. Throughout, I’ll highlight safe diagnostic practices so your investigation does not increase load on a struggling system. By the end of the lesson series you’ll be able to compose KQL joins that join AzureMetrics with AzureDiagnostics, find deadlock evidence, interpret wait statistics, and pick a tracing strategy with Application Insights. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you reach for when a single slow user transaction hides a multi-component problem.

screens.title: Kusto Query Language for Correlation
screens.narratorSegment: Kusto Query Language is the primary tool you’ll use inside Log Analytics when correlating metrics and diagnostic logs. At its core KQL is a read-only, pipe-based language that lets you filter, project, parse, and summarize streaming log data. For advanced troubleshooting you will use let statements to define thresholds and windows, parse expressions to extract fields from message text, and joins to bring together AzureMetrics and AzureDiagnostics records so you can see which queries were running during metric spikes. A concrete example is defining a C P U threshold and summarizing metric bins, then joining that time window to QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics to find top C P U-consuming queries during spikes. A common misconception is that a single slow query explains every spike; correlation often reveals many queries together, or infrastructure issues like input and output bursts. Practice: write a let for a cpuThreshold and a timeWindow, then capture the metric spikes and join diagnostics filtered by the same resource and time. Key takeaway: KQL turns separate telemetry streams into evidence you can act on. When you build queries, prefer narrow time windows and limited summarization when systems are under stress to avoid adding load.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › KQL Fundamentals
Definition & Core Operators
  • let: name an expression or window for reuse.
  • parse: extract structured fields from message text.
  • summarize: aggregate values over bins or groups.
  • join: correlate two tables by resource and time.
Concrete example
Define a CPU threshold and find top queries during spikes by joining AzureMetrics and AzureDiagnostics within the same time window.
Key Takeaway

KQL makes correlation explicit: name windows, extract fields, and join by resource and time to turn telemetry into root-cause evidence.

Common misconception
Assuming a single slow query is the entire cause. Often spikes include multiple queries or infrastructure bottlenecks like I/O bursts.
Try this pattern
  1. Define thresholds and a lookback using let statements.
  2. Find metric bins that exceed thresholds with summarize.
  3. Join diagnostics filtered by the same resource and time window.
  4. Order by aggregated CPU or duration to find top offenders.
Scenario Card
During an evening spike you correlate CPU percent rising above 80% with several queries that together consumed most CPU; optimization reduced the peak.

screens.title: KQL Deep Dive: Correlate CPU Spikes with Top Queries
screens.narratorSegment: We will walk through a practical KQL query that finds C P U spikes and the top queries active during those spikes. First, the query defines a cpuThreshold and a timeWindow with let statements — this creates a named threshold and keeps the rest of the query readable. Next, it reads AzureMetrics and filters by the S Q L resource provider and metric name, then finds bins where the maximum exceeded the threshold. The query extends the spike windows slightly to include surrounding events. Then it joins the spike windows to AzureDiagnostics, filtering for QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics and parsing the Message to extract query and plan hashes and average C P U times. Finally the inner summarize aggregates C P U by query hash per resource and the outer join returns rows where diagnostics fall inside the spike window. A common pitfall is joining on coarse timestamps; ensure you bin times consistently and use the extended window so you don’t miss queries that began slightly earlier. Practice writing a smaller version first with take 50 and short time ranges to avoid heavy load.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › KQL Deep Dive
Example KQL
This is a complete example to run in Log Analytics. When systems are strained, add | take 50 or narrow the time range.
// Example KQL: Correlate high CPU with top queries for Azure SQL Database
let cpuThreshold = 80; // Define CPU threshold
let timeWindow = 1h;   // Look back 1 hour

// Get CPU spikes
let cpuSpikes = AzureMetrics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.SQL" and MetricName == "cpu_percent"
| where Maximum > cpuThreshold
| summarize StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), Resource
| extend StartTime = StartTime - 5m, EndTime = EndTime + 5m;

// Get top queries during CPU spikes
cpuSpikes
| join kind=inner (
    AzureDiagnostics
    | where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.SQL" and Category == "QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics"
    | parse Message with * "query_hash_text: " QueryHashText:string ", query_plan_hash_text: " QueryPlanHashText:string ", avg_cpu_time: " AvgCpuTime:long *
    | project TimeGenerated, Resource, QueryHashText, QueryPlanHashText, AvgCpuTime
    | summarize TotalAvgCpuTime = sum(AvgCpuTime) by QueryHashText, QueryPlanHashText, Resource, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | order by TotalAvgCpuTime desc
) on Resource
| where TimeGenerated between (StartTime .. EndTime)
| project TimeGenerated, Resource, QueryHashText, QueryPlanHashText, TotalAvgCpuTime, CpuSpikeStartTime = StartTime, CpuSpikeEndTime = EndTime
| order by TimeGenerated asc;
Annotated steps
  • let names the threshold and window to keep the rest readable.
  • AzureMetrics identifies metric spikes by maximum value and bins time.
  • parse Message extracts query and plan hashes from diagnostics.
  • join matches spikes to diagnostics by Resource and overlapping time.
Pro tip
When you expect high volume, run the inner diagnostics query with | take 100 or with a narrower time filter before joining to avoid heavy join costs.
Key Takeaway

Annotate queries with let and careful time bins. Parse diagnostics for meaningful identifiers and avoid broad joins in production without sampling.

screens.title: Correlating Application Errors with Database Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When application errors occur, correlation inside the same Log Analytics workspace rapidly reveals whether the database contributed. Start by defining the application error set — for example, AppServiceHTTPLogs where HTTP status is 500 or greater. Next, construct a database issue set: AzureDiagnostics filtered for Errors or slow queries based on parsed avg_cpu_time or duration. Third, normalize resource identifiers so AppResource and DbResource match; often the same resource name appears in both tables. Fourth, join the two sets on resource and a short time window — one minute is a practical starting point — to find pairs of application errors and database events that occurred within the same minute. A misconception is to assume correlation implies causation; correlation narrows suspects, but you still need to inspect the traces and user flows. In practice, use | project to show times and messages, and order by time to examine the sequence. If you find repeated matches, instrument that application call path with a trace id for future deterministic linking. Correlating Application Errors with Database Issues means define app errors and database issues, normalize resource identity, and join within a short time window to see coincident events that narrow root-cause candidates.. In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern to find whether application errors coincide with database problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step-by-step cards

Identify application error logs and database diagnostics tables.

screens.title: Deadlocks: Detection and Interpretation
screens.narratorSegment: A deadlock happens when two or more transactions hold locks the others need, creating a circular wait so none can proceed. The engine resolves this by choosing one transaction as the deadlock victim and terminating it. Deadlocks produce artifacts you can analyze: deadlock graphs or XML recorded in diagnostic streams. In Azure S Q L, deadlock data appears in the system_health extended event session and can be sent to Log Analytics with SQLInsights. For PostgreSQL, you need log_lock_waits enabled to record lock waits in server logs; for MySQL the server status or the output of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS can reveal deadlock information. Resolving deadlocks often requires identifying the locking resources and changing transaction ordering, reducing transaction scope, or lowering isolation levels where appropriate. A common misconception is to simply retry failed transactions without fixing the locking pattern — retries can mask systemic concurrency issues and create additional load. The practical approach is to extract the deadlock graph, map the queries and objects involved, and change the code or schema to avoid circular locking. Deadlocks: Detection and Interpretation means deadlocks are circular lock waits; examine deadlock graphs or log entries to identify resources and change transaction ordering or isolation to prevent recurrence.. In practical terms, what a deadlock is, where to find its evidence, and how to resolve it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Deadlocks
What is a deadlock?

Two or more transactions hold locks the other needs, forming a circular wait. The engine resolves by killing a victim, which appears as an error to the application.

Where to find evidence
  • Azure SQL: system_health extended events or SQLInsights forwarded to Log Analytics.
  • PostgreSQL: server logs when log_lock_waits is enabled.
  • MySQL: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS output for deadlock details.
Analysis pattern
  1. Retrieve deadlock artifact (XML or log text).
  2. Identify victim and the locking queries with object ids.
  3. Map queries to application code paths.
  4. Change locking order, reduce transaction scope, or lower isolation where safe.
Scenario
Two services update overlapping rows in different orders. A deadlock graph shows the circular locks; changing both services to update rows in the same order removed the deadlocks.

screens.title: Querying Deadlock Records in Log Analytics
screens.narratorSegment: When you suspect deadlocks, start by querying AzureDiagnostics for entries categorized as Deadlock or for the deadlock XML stored in message fields. A straightforward KQL pattern filters ResourceProvider for the S Q L provider and Category for deadlock, projects the TimeGenerated, Resource, and Message fields and orders by time. This returns raw XML blobs you can inspect or parse. The raw XML contains the victim and the processes involved; parsing can extract query text or object ids. A common mistake is searching only for error codes without checking diagnostic categories — deadlock artifacts are often labeled as a separate category or contained in system extended events. For MySQL or PostgreSQL, where deadlocks appear in server logs, forward those logs to Log Analytics and use similar filtering. After retrieving the XML, copy it into a deadlock visualizer or parse it with KQL functions if small. Remember safety: limit your returned rows or restrict time ranges to avoid scanning months of logs in production. Querying Deadlock Records in Log Analytics means filter azurediagnostics for deadlock categories, project the xml message, and parse the artifact to identify victims and locking queries while keeping queries limited for production safety.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Deadlock Retrieval
Simple KQL to find deadlocks
AzureDiagnostics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.SQL" and Category == "Deadlock"
| project TimeGenerated, Resource, DeadlockXml = Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
| take 50
This retrieves recent deadlock XML blobs. Use take and date filters to limit load.
Next steps after retrieval
  • Copy XML into a deadlock visualizer to view the lock graph.
  • Parse XML to extract victim's session id and involved SQL text.
  • Map session ids back to application traces or connection strings to find the calling code.
Safety note
Avoid scanning large time ranges in production. Use precise filters and | take to reduce diagnostic load.

screens.title: Resource Contention: CPU, I/O, Memory, Locks
screens.narratorSegment: Resource contention can point at C P U, input and output, memory, or locks; each shows different signals. C P U contention appears as sustained high C P U percent in metrics. input and output contention commonly appears as high IOPS, elevated latency, or IO_LATCH waits reported in wait statistics. Memory pressure may present as increased paging or lower buffer pool hit rates. Lock contention appears as blocking chains, long waits for locks, or deadlocks. To diagnose, look at the right sources: AzureMetrics for time-series C P U and IOPS; wait statistics and sys views for lock and wait types; pg_stat_activity for PostgreSQL active queries and waits; and SHOW PROCESSLIST for MySQL to see live sessions. A typical misconception is to always scale up when seeing high C P U. Sometimes query optimization or index tuning reduces C P U and input and output without changing capacity. Also, if waits show IO_LATCH, scaling compute alone won't solve underlying storage latency issues. Use combined evidence — metrics, diagnostics, and process views — to determine whether to optimize queries, add resources, or both.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Resource Contention
CPU Contention
Metric signal: sustained high cpu_percent. Look for heavy query CPU time in diagnostics and Query Store.
I/O Contention
Signal: high IOPS, elevated latency, IO_LATCH or read/write waits. Investigate storage tier and query patterns causing reads/writes.
Memory Pressure
Signal: low buffer hit rates, paging, elevated memory usage. Consider cache sizing and query plans that cause spills.
Lock Contention
Signal: blocking chains, long wait times for locks, or deadlocks. Use wait stats and diagnostic logs to find culprits.
Where to inspect
AzureMetrics, wait statistics, sys views, pg_stat_activity, and SHOW PROCESSLIST are the primary sources for each engine.
Decision tip
Optimize queries and indexes first for recurring patterns; scale when usage exceeds service tier limits or optimization cannot remove contention.

screens.title: Interpreting Wait Statistics and Server Views

For PostgreSQL, pg_stat_activity shows active queries, their states, and waiting reasons. MySQL’s process list can show long-running statements and locks. Start by capturing a snapshot of waits and ordering by total wait time or average wait per request. If IO_LATCH or PAGEIOLATCH waits dominate, storage latency is a likely culprit; if CXPACKET or C P U-related waits dominate, parallelism or compute limits may need attention. When you see lock waits, drill into the sessions holding locks and the S Q L text to understand the locking pattern. A misconception is treating waits as absolute proof of the resource to increase; waits can be symptoms of inefficient queries causing excessive IO or memory churn. Use wait stats together with query plans, diagnostics, and metrics to decide whether to tune S Q L, add indexes, or increase capacity. Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Wait Statistics
Snapshot checklist
  1. Capture waits ordered by total wait time.
  2. Identify dominant wait types (IO, lock, CPU-related).
  3. Map waits to active sessions or query plans.
  4. Decide: tune query, change indexing, or scale resources.
Example
High IO waits plus scans in query plans point to missing indexes. Adding an index reduced IO and wait time in subsequent runs.
Common pitfall
Seeing high CPU waits and immediately scaling up without checking query plans can waste cost. First verify whether inefficient plans or parallelism are the root cause.
Pro tip

Capture short, targeted snapshots while adding minimal overhead: filter to busy databases and avoid full-history scans during peak load.

screens.title: Distributed Tracing for End-to-End Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed tracing links a single user request as it traverses services and databases so you can see where time is spent. Application Insights collects spans and operations from instrumented services and can correlate those spans with backend calls to the database. Databases do not always emit trace spans by themselves, so instrument the application stack to include database calls as part of a trace. A trace will show a parent request and child spans representing service-to-service calls and database interactions. This helps when individual database queries look fast in isolation but overall request latency accumulates across many small calls. A common error is assuming tracing is only for apps; it is a debugging amplifier for databases too, since you can link slow user experiences to database calls recorded as spans. Start by instrumenting a few critical endpoints and include a correlation id in logs and custom metrics so application logs, traces, and database diagnostics can be stitched together for a full picture. Tracing does not replace metrics or diagnostics; it complements them by showing the user-perceived path and time distribution, helping to map metrics to code paths.

screens.title: Custom Metrics and Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Default telemetry is often sufficient for basic monitoring, but custom metrics and logs capture application-specific behavior that matters for troubleshooting. Custom metrics can include business counters, user transaction durations, or queue lengths. Custom logs might include enriched context such as user ids, correlation ids, or domain-specific error codes. In Azure Monitor you can send these custom metrics and custom log records to Log Analytics where they can be correlated with AzureMetrics and AzureDiagnostics. A key example is emitting the user transaction id as a custom property in both application logs and a custom metric so you can quickly join related records. Avoid high-cardinality fields in metrics that can explode storage and query costs. A common pitfall is instrumenting everything without a retention or aggregation plan; decide which metrics need high resolution versus those sampled at lower frequency. Custom telemetry helps you track issues that default telemetry misses, making targeted KQL queries faster and more meaningful. screens.title: Capacity Planning and Scaling Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Capacity planning uses historical metric trends to forecast when your database will need more compute, storage, or parallelism. Start by collecting trends for C P U, memory, IOPS, and storage growth over meaningful windows — days, weeks, and months. If databases regularly hit thresholds like 80 percent C P U during peak hours, plan scaling before service impact. There are two principal options: scale up, which increases resources for a single instance, and scale out, which distributes workload across multiple instances via read replicas or sharding. The choice depends on workload characteristics: write-heavy transactional workloads often benefit from scale up, whereas read-heavy workloads can often use read replicas. A practical approach is to combine gradual scaling with optimization: first examine whether indexing or query tuning reduces trend growth. Azure Advisor can give recommendations based on usage patterns, but use it as input, not as the sole decision maker. Finally, always test scaling changes under load in a staging environment if possible, and monitor after the change to validate the expected effect. Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Capacity Planning
Trend analysis timeline
  1. Collect daily and weekly metrics for CPU, IOPS, memory, and storage growth.
  2. Identify peak-hour percentiles (e.g., 95th percentile CPU).
  3. Project growth to forecast when thresholds will be reached.
Decision framework
If write-heavy and CPU-limited, scale up. If read-heavy, consider read replicas. Always attempt tuning before costly scaling.
Practical steps

  • Test scaling in staging, monitor the impact, and revert if required.
  • Combine scaling with index and query tuning for cost-efficiency.
Key Takeaway

Forecast using percentiles and storage growth, test scaling actions, and prioritize optimization before capacity increases when possible.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move beyond simple dashboards and learn how to investigate complex performance problems across Azure databases. You will learn to use Kusto Query Language to correlate metrics and logs, to identify which queries or resources caused spikes, and to extract deadlock graphs from diagnostic streams. We’ll look at how resource contention can hide behind fast single-query timings, why distributed tracing is essential in microservices, and how custom metrics and logs let you observe behaviors not exposed by default telemetry. A practical outcome is capacity planning: using trend analysis to decide when to scale up or scale out before production impact. Throughout, I’ll highlight safe diagnostic practices so your investigation does not increase load on a struggling system. By the end of the lesson series you’ll be able to compose KQL joins that join AzureMetrics with AzureDiagnostics, find deadlock evidence, interpret wait statistics, and pick a tracing strategy with Application Insights. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you reach for when a single slow user transaction hides a multi-component problem.

This first objectives slide describes the core analytical skills you’ll build. First, you will perform advanced analysis using Kusto Query Language in Log Analytics to correlate metrics and logs. That means learning to write let statements, joins, parsing expressions, and summarization to surface which queries ran during spikes. Second, you will troubleshoot complex performance problems such as deadlocks and resource contention by retrieving diagnostic streams and interpreting deadlock graphs or wait statistics. You will learn where deadlock XML lives and how to extract the victim and locking queries. Third, you will understand the principles of distributed tracing so you can see an end-to-end request path across services and the database. And fourth, you will implement custom metrics and logs to capture application-specific behavior that built-in telemetry misses. These skills let you move from reactive alerts to deliberate root-cause workflows and better capacity planning.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied investigative skills. You will learn to correlate application errors with database issues by joining application logs with database diagnostics inside the same Log Analytics workspace. You will safely extract deadlock information with queries that filter deadlock categories or parse XML stored in diagnostic messages. You will interpret server-side wait statistics and corresponding server views such as pg_stat_activity or process lists, enabling you to distinguish input and output or C P U bottlenecks from locking issues. Additionally, you will implement custom telemetry so your monitoring includes application context — for example tracing a user transaction id through logs and metrics. Finally, you’ll practice safe diagnostics: when systems are strained, use limits and small sampling queries to avoid adding load. These applied outcomes move you from knowledge to trusted troubleshooting practice.

Kusto Query Language is the primary tool you’ll use inside Log Analytics when correlating metrics and diagnostic logs. At its core KQL is a read-only, pipe-based language that lets you filter, project, parse, and summarize streaming log data. For advanced troubleshooting you will use let statements to define thresholds and windows, parse expressions to extract fields from message text, and joins to bring together AzureMetrics and AzureDiagnostics records so you can see which queries were running during metric spikes. A concrete example is defining a C P U threshold and summarizing metric bins, then joining that time window to QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics to find top C P U-consuming queries during spikes. A common misconception is that a single slow query explains every spike; correlation often reveals many queries together, or infrastructure issues like input and output bursts. Practice: write a let for a cpuThreshold and a timeWindow, then capture the metric spikes and join diagnostics filtered by the same resource and time. Key takeaway: KQL turns separate telemetry streams into evidence you can act on. When you build queries, prefer narrow time windows and limited summarization when systems are under stress to avoid adding load.

We will walk through a practical KQL query that finds C P U spikes and the top queries active during those spikes. First, the query defines a cpuThreshold and a timeWindow with let statements — this creates a named threshold and keeps the rest of the query readable. Next, it reads AzureMetrics and filters by the S Q L resource provider and metric name, then finds bins where the maximum exceeded the threshold. The query extends the spike windows slightly to include surrounding events. Then it joins the spike windows to AzureDiagnostics, filtering for QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics and parsing the Message to extract query and plan hashes and average C P U times. Finally the inner summarize aggregates C P U by query hash per resource and the outer join returns rows where diagnostics fall inside the spike window. A common pitfall is joining on coarse timestamps; ensure you bin times consistently and use the extended window so you don’t miss queries that began slightly earlier. Practice writing a smaller version first with take 50 and short time ranges to avoid heavy load.

When application errors occur, correlation inside the same Log Analytics workspace rapidly reveals whether the database contributed. Start by defining the application error set — for example, AppServiceHTTPLogs where HTTP status is 500 or greater. Next, construct a database issue set: AzureDiagnostics filtered for Errors or slow queries based on parsed avg_cpu_time or duration. Third, normalize resource identifiers so AppResource and DbResource match; often the same resource name appears in both tables. Fourth, join the two sets on resource and a short time window — one minute is a practical starting point — to find pairs of application errors and database events that occurred within the same minute. A misconception is to assume correlation implies causation; correlation narrows suspects, but you still need to inspect the traces and user flows. In practice, use | project to show times and messages, and order by time to examine the sequence. If you find repeated matches, instrument that application call path with a trace id for future deterministic linking. Correlating Application Errors with Database Issues means define app errors and database issues, normalize resource identity, and join within a short time window to see coincident events that narrow root-cause candidates.. In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern to find whether application errors coincide with database problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A deadlock happens when two or more transactions hold locks the others need, creating a circular wait so none can proceed. The engine resolves this by choosing one transaction as the deadlock victim and terminating it. Deadlocks produce artifacts you can analyze: deadlock graphs or XML recorded in diagnostic streams. In Azure S Q L, deadlock data appears in the system_health extended event session and can be sent to Log Analytics with SQLInsights. For PostgreSQL, you need log_lock_waits enabled to record lock waits in server logs; for MySQL the server status or the output of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS can reveal deadlock information. Resolving deadlocks often requires identifying the locking resources and changing transaction ordering, reducing transaction scope, or lowering isolation levels where appropriate. A common misconception is to simply retry failed transactions without fixing the locking pattern — retries can mask systemic concurrency issues and create additional load. The practical approach is to extract the deadlock graph, map the queries and objects involved, and change the code or schema to avoid circular locking. In practical terms, what a deadlock is, where to find its evidence, and how to resolve it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you suspect deadlocks, start by querying AzureDiagnostics for entries categorized as Deadlock or for the deadlock XML stored in message fields. A straightforward KQL pattern filters ResourceProvider for the S Q L provider and Category for deadlock, projects the TimeGenerated, Resource, and Message fields and orders by time. This returns raw XML blobs you can inspect or parse. The raw XML contains the victim and the processes involved; parsing can extract query text or object ids. A common mistake is searching only for error codes without checking diagnostic categories — deadlock artifacts are often labeled as a separate category or contained in system extended events. For MySQL or PostgreSQL, where deadlocks appear in server logs, forward those logs to Log Analytics and use similar filtering. After retrieving the XML, copy it into a deadlock visualizer or parse it with KQL functions if small. Remember safety: limit your returned rows or restrict time ranges to avoid scanning months of logs in production. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

C P U contention appears as sustained high C P U percent in metrics. input and output contention commonly appears as high IOPS, elevated latency, or IO_LATCH waits reported in wait statistics. Memory pressure may present as increased paging or lower buffer pool hit rates. Lock contention appears as blocking chains, long waits for locks, or deadlocks. To diagnose, look at the right sources: AzureMetrics for time-series C P U and IOPS; wait statistics and sys views for lock and wait types; pg_stat_activity for PostgreSQL active queries and waits; and SHOW PROCESSLIST for MySQL to see live sessions. A typical misconception is to always scale up when seeing high C P U. Sometimes query optimization or index tuning reduces C P U and input and output without changing capacity. Also, if waits show IO_LATCH, scaling compute alone won't solve underlying storage latency issues. Use combined evidence — metrics, diagnostics, and process views — to determine whether to optimize queries, add resources, or both.

This helps when individual database queries look fast in isolation but overall request latency accumulates across many small calls. A common error is assuming tracing is only for apps; it is a debugging amplifier for databases too, since you can link slow user experiences to database calls recorded as spans. Default telemetry is often sufficient for basic monitoring, but custom metrics and logs capture application-specific behavior that matters for troubleshooting. Custom metrics can include business counters, user transaction durations, or queue lengths. Custom logs might include enriched context such as user ids, correlation ids, or domain-specific error codes. In Azure Monitor you can send these custom metrics and custom log records to Log Analytics where they can be correlated with AzureMetrics and AzureDiagnostics. A key example is emitting the user transaction id as a custom property in both application logs and a custom metric so you can quickly join related records. Avoid high-cardinality fields in metrics that can explode storage and query costs. A common pitfall is instrumenting everything without a retention or aggregation plan; decide which metrics need high resolution versus those sampled at lower frequency. Custom telemetry helps you track issues that default telemetry misses, making targeted KQL queries faster and more meaningful. Capacity planning uses historical metric trends to forecast when your database will need more compute, storage, or parallelism. Start by collecting trends for C P U, memory, IOPS, and storage growth over meaningful windows — days, weeks, and months. If databases regularly hit thresholds like 80 percent C P U during peak hours, plan scaling before service impact. There are two principal options: scale up, which increases resources for a single instance, and scale out, which distributes workload across multiple instances via read replicas or sharding. The choice depends on workload characteristics: write-heavy transactional workloads often benefit from scale up, whereas read-heavy workloads can often use read replicas. A practical approach is to combine gradual scaling with optimization: first examine whether indexing or query tuning reduces trend growth. Azure Advisor can give recommendations based on usage patterns, but use it as input, not as the sole decision maker. Finally, always test scaling changes under load in a staging environment if possible, and monitor after the change to validate the expected effect. Let’s consolidate the essential concepts you’ll use daily. First, Kusto Query Language is your tool for advanced correlation: use let, parse, summarize, and join to combine metrics and diagnostics.
